overview: Sigma 4.11's WorldTime is an unimplemented stub. The module registers for EventTick and EventPacket, and its onEvent body contains both branches completely empty: the EventTick case and the EventPacket case each do nothing. The identical empty shell ships in Sigma 2.08 and 3.9, so the module has never had behavior in the public lineage; it appears to be a placeholder for a time-of-day override that was never filled in. A functional WorldTime would sit in the S03 path - the fork's NetHandlerPlayClient.handleTimeUpdate applies the server's world time through WorldClient.func_82738_a and setWorldTime - rewriting or freezing the packet's two long fields (world time and total world time) or the client's clock. As shipped, the module consumes events and discards them: the S03 stream reaches the handler untouched, the world clock runs exactly as the server dictates, and the module's wire footprint is zero.

sections.p: onEvent is registered for both EventTick.class and EventPacket.class via @RegisterEvent, and the instanceof dispatch splits on the event type. Both branches are empty blocks: the EventTick case contains a blank statement and the EventPacket case contains a blank statement. There is no field access, no mc reference beyond the inherited Module base, no packet mutation, and no setting registration. The module contributes nothing to any event it receives; the only observable behavior is the dispatch itself.

sections.h: Where a WorldTime would have hooked in
sections.p: The fork's NetHandlerPlayClient.handleTimeUpdate (line 835) is the S03 consumer: it calls theWorld.func_82738_a(packetIn.func_149366_c()) to set the total world time and theWorld.setWorldTime(packetIn.func_149365_d()) to set the day phase. S03PacketTimeUpdate carries two longs - the world time and the total world time, with the total negated when the doDaylightCycle flag is false - read from the buffer in readPacketData. A time module in this lineage would either intercept the S03 in the EventPacket branch (which NetworkManager fires in channelRead0 before the handler) and rewrite the fields, or re-set the world clock from the EventTick branch. The empty branches mean neither hook exists; the S03 is processed by handleTimeUpdate with the server's values.

There is none. The module sends no packets, cancels no packets, and rewrites no fields, so the S03 stream is byte-identical to an unmodified client's. The honest fingerprint of the module is the absence of one: the world time on the client equals the server's, day cycles run on schedule, and nothing in the packet log distinguishes the module from being disabled.

files.label: WorldTime.java
files.explanation: The module is this file alone, authored by Arithmo on 5/6/2017, and it is a skeleton. The constructor passes ModuleData through to the superclass; onEvent is annotated for EventTick and EventPacket, and its if/else-if dispatch contains two empty branches. Nothing is read, written, cancelled or sent in either case. The same file - byte-for-byte the same empty body - ships in the Sigma 2.08 and 3.9 trees, which confirms the stub is not a 4.11 regression but the module's permanent state in the public lineage. The registration of both event types is the only signal of intent: the module was meant to act on the tick loop, the packet stream, or both, and neither action was ever written. Any time-of-day functionality would have to be added here.

files.label: S03PacketTimeUpdate.java (the packet a WorldTime would touch)
files.explanation: This is the packet class in the module's domain, and it shows exactly what a working WorldTime would rewrite. The class holds two longs: field_149369_a, the current world time (day phase), and field_149368_b, the total world time, which the constructor negates when the doDaylightCycle flag is false (a negative total freezes the cycle). readPacketData reads both longs from the buffer and writePacketData writes them back. The fork's handleTimeUpdate consumes them through func_149366_c() and func_149365_d() to drive WorldClient's clock. Because S03 is clientbound and its payload only feeds local rendering, a module that rewrote these fields (or the world clock after them) would change nothing the server can observe - which is the point the countering section makes: even a completed WorldTime would have no anticheat counter, because no anticheat inspects the S03 payload. As shipped, of course, the module never touches the packet at all.

countering.label: PacketFrequency (general packet-rate ledger)
countering.explanation:
PacketFrequency is NCP's general volume guard: every qualifying packet adds a point to data.packetFrequency, and the check scores the bucket window into packets-per-second (score * 1000 / window duration), flagging when the rate exceeds cc.packetFrequencyPacketsPerSecond, with a TickTask lag adjustment before the actions fire.

It is included here as the nearest general stream guard, and the honest finding is that it cannot see the module in either direction. The ledger counts only the serverbound packets NCP chooses to feed it (keepalives, transactions and flying packets, per NetStatic's wiring), while the module's domain - the clientbound S03 time stream - never enters it, and the shipped stub emits nothing at all. The check's existence is the closest NCP comes to policing the volume of traffic the module's domain lives in, which is to say it polices the wrong direction and the wrong side.

countering.label: FlyingFrequency (C03 rate)
countering.explanation:
FlyingFrequency bounds the rate of C03 flying packets: each one adds a point to data.flyingFrequencyAll, the check divides the window score by cc.flyingFrequencySeconds for a packets-per-second figure, and flags when it exceeds cc.flyingFrequencyPPS.

Like PacketFrequency it is a serverbound-rate guard, and like PacketFrequency it is doubly irrelevant to WorldTime: it observes only the C03 stream the module never touches, and the S03 time packets flow the other way entirely. The two NCP rate checks together establish the shape of NCP's packet layer - volume-based, serverbound-only - which has no concept of a clientbound packet's payload. There is no NCP check on world time because there is nothing in NCP's model of a cheater that involves it.

countering.label: Arc v2 (no S03 consumer)
countering.explanation:
Arc v2's PacketListener enumerates every packet the anticheat subscribes to, and the list is entirely serverbound: FLYING, POSITION and POSITION_LOOK for the movement layer, USE_ENTITY, ARM_ANIMATION, HELD_ITEM_SLOT and BLOCK_PLACE for combat and soup handling. There is no Play.Server adapter of any kind, so S03PacketTimeUpdate is not merely unchecked - it is never even seen by the anticheat's packet pipeline.

The entry documents the strongest possible statement about WorldTime: the module's entire domain is invisible to Arc v2 because Arc v2 observes no clientbound packets at all. Combined with the two NCP rate checks, the countering picture is complete - of the anticheats in this reference set, none inspects the S03 payload or the client's world clock, which is why a time-override module, implemented or not, has no anticheat counter. World time is cosmetic state the server broadcasts and trusts the client to render; the stub's emptiness changes nothing about that.
